interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Scientific Agent Skills: A Library of Procedural Knowledge for Research Agents
papers.authors: Timothy Kassis , Vinayak Agarwal , Yuhuan He , Darshil Patel , Aubrey M. Brueckner
papers.abstract: A language-model agent asked to analyse an experiment will usually return working code. Whether the analysis is defensible is a different question. A defensible analysis depends on procedural choices: which test the field accepts, which identifier namespace is authoritative, and which caveats must accompany a result. We present Scientific Agent Skills, an open library of 163 such procedures in 16 areas of practice, including genomics, cheminformatics, medical imaging, study design and scientific communication. Each skill is a directory built around a versioned, human-readable instruction file. An agent loads the file only when a task calls for it; the directory often also contains reference material and runnable scripts. We report no task-level evaluation and no host selection rate. Openly licensed and available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant to LLM agents for scientific workflows, providing a library of procedural knowledge that could enhance research agents in astronomy. The focus on defensible analyses and field-accepted procedures aligns with reproducible research interests.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem that language-model agents often return working code but not analyses that are defensible according to field standards. It introduces an open library of 163 procedural skills, each with a human-readable instruction file that agents load on demand, covering areas like study design and scientific communication. For astronomy, this could help agents follow best practices in data analysis, such as using authoritative catalogs or standard SED-fitting procedures. I could imagine using it to build an agent that performs literature review or data reduction with built-in checks for methodological correctness. However, the paper reports no task-level evaluation, so its practical utility remains unproven and needs testing.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the library includes any astronomy or astrophysics-specific skills
Look for examples of how a skill is structured and loaded by an agent
Assess the licensing and ease of adapting skills to custom research workflows

papers.title: Explore Before Committing: Hypothesis-Guided Search for Deep Research Agents
papers.authors: Ruochen Zhou , Zhengyu Chen , Luan Zhang , Siyang Gao , Yee Whye Teh , Shiqi Chen
papers.abstract: Deep-research agents answer complex questions by interacting with search and browsing tools, yet they often search along a single evolving trajectory. Our trajectory-level analysis reveals a common failure mode in which the agent may encounter an early search state with several plausible directions, but follow one direction before collecting enough comparative evidence. Once this happens, subsequent tool calls tend to reinforce the same path, increasing the chance of failure when the initial direction is misleading. We further find that successful trajectories reduce this risk through two behaviors: grounding vague exploration in concrete candidates and shifting directions when the current path is weak or incomplete. Based on these findings, we propose HypoSearch, which generates lightweight hypotheses as soft search hints, explores them through bounded independent branches, and compares branch-level evidence before commitment. Across four deep-research benchmarks and three backbone models, HypoSearch consistently outperforms single-trajectory search and standard parallel baselines, improving Qwen3.5-122B from 46.7 to 60.0 on BC-small while using fewer tool calls than five independent trajectories. A pilot supervised fine-tuning study further shows that these behavioral signals can curate compact training trajectories and reduce degradation from unfiltered data.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant to deep research agents, which could be used for literature review and automated scientific discovery in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses a failure mode in deep-research agents where they commit to an early search direction without gathering enough comparative evidence. The main idea is to generate lightweight hypotheses as soft search hints, explore them in bounded independent branches, and compare evidence before committing, improving search efficiency and accuracy. For astronomy, this is highly relevant because it could enhance research agents that search literature or data for astrophysical questions, such as finding properties of high-redshift galaxies. A concrete workflow could be using such an agent to conduct a systematic literature review on little red dots or AGN properties. The caveat is that the method is tested on general benchmarks, not astronomy-specific, so it needs validation on domain-specific search tasks.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for details on how hypotheses are generated and how branch exploration is bounded
Check if the method could be adapted to search astronomical databases or literature
See if the training data or benchmarks include any scientific domains

papers.title: Beyond Language Priors: Diagnosing and Fixing Visual-Origin Hallucinations in Multimodal LLM
papers.authors: Peiyang Xu , Xiaopei Zhu , Jun Zhu , Xiaolin Hu
papers.abstract: Existing research on object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) predominantly attributes the problem to language priors such as over-reliance on textual co-occurrence statistics. We challenge this view by presenting quantitative evidence for a complementary, under-explored cause: visual-origin hallucination, where hallucinations arise from incorrect visual feature extraction and misalignment between image and text embeddings. Through cosine similarity analysis and Smooth Grad-CAM entropy measurements, we show that hallucinated samples exhibit systematically lower image-text similarity (average 0.158 vs. -0.122) and inverted attention patterns, where attention is dispersed when the target object is present but wrongly concentrated when it is absent. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose Adversarial Contrastive Fine-Tuning (ACFT). ACFT uses an Adversarial Hallucination Attribute Flipping (AHAF) procedure, involving minimal, targeted adversarial perturbations that flip an image's hallucination attribute, to construct perfectly aligned positive-negative pairs, which are then used for contrastive fine-tuning. AHAF simultaneously serves as a diagnostic probe, revealing that MLLM visual representations lie dangerously close to hallucination decision boundaries. Requiring only 0.9% of the COCO dataset and adding zero inference overhead, ACFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on POPE, MME, and four description-level hallucination benchmarks across LLaVA, MiniGPT-4, and Qwen2.5-VL. Code is available at this https URL
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses visual-origin hallucinations in multimodal LLMs, which is crucial for reliable analysis of astronomical images where subtle features may be misrepresented. The proposed ACFT method for reducing hallucinations could improve trust in LMM outputs for JWST data interpretation.
papers.Short digest: This paper challenges the common belief that hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are solely due to language priors, showing instead that incorrect visual feature extraction and image-text misalignment also play a key role. The authors introduce Adversarial Contrastive Fine-Tuning (ACFT), which uses targeted adversarial perturbations to create aligned positive-negative pairs for contrastive learning, reducing hallucinations without extra inference cost. For astronomy, this matters because LMMs are increasingly used to interpret JWST images, and reducing visual-origin hallucinations could make their outputs more reliable for tasks like identifying high-redshift galaxies or AGN. A practical workflow could involve fine-tuning an LMM on astronomical image-caption pairs with ACFT to improve accuracy in source classification. However, the method is tested on COCO, so its transferability to astronomical data needs validation, and the adversarial perturbations may not capture the unique noise characteristics of JWST images.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the ACFT method is evaluated on any non-COCO datasets or if the authors discuss domain transfer limitations.
Look for details on how the adversarial perturbations are generated and whether they could be adapted to astronomical image noise properties.
Examine the diagnostic metrics (cosine similarity, Smooth Grad-CAM) for evidence that visual-origin hallucinations are indeed reduced in practice.

papers.title: SCoNE: Selective Context-aware Neuron Editing for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is highly sensitive to retrieval noise: when retrieved documents mix informative and irrelevant context, LLMs are easily distracted, leading to hallucinations. To overcome this, we propose SCoNE (Selective Context-aware Neuron Editing), a training-free model editing approach that improves retrieval noise robustness by selectively strengthening context-aware FFN neurons that are identified by both high attribution and high cross-input variability. SCoNE requires only a small number of mining samples, no fine-tuning, and no inference-time overhead. Across various knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks and two LLM backbones, SCoNE consistently outperforms competitive baseline methods. Our code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Addresses retrieval noise robustness in RAG, which is directly relevant to using LLMs for literature review and data analysis in astronomy, where retrieved documents can be noisy.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of retrieval noise in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), where irrelevant context can distract LLMs and cause hallucinations. The main idea is SCoNE, a training-free method that selectively edits feed-forward neurons in LLMs to strengthen context-aware processing, identified by high attribution and cross-input variability. For astronomy, this is relevant because when using RAG for literature review or data analysis, retrieved papers or catalogs may contain irrelevant information. The workflow could involve applying SCoNE to improve the robustness of an astronomy-focused RAG system that retrieves papers or data descriptions. However, the method requires mining samples and may need adaptation to astronomical text, and its effectiveness on domain-specific corpora is untested.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is evaluated on any scientific or domain-specific question-answering tasks.
Look for details on how many mining samples are needed and whether they can be obtained from astronomical literature.
Examine if the neuron editing is stable across different prompts and domains.

papers.title: Agentic Multimodal Models for Environmental Hyperspectral Unmixing
papers.authors: Michał Cholewa , Luca Ciampi , Nicola Messina , Przemysław Głomb , Giuseppe Amato
papers.abstract: Hyperspectral unmixing is a key task in remote sensing that aims to decompose mixed pixels in hyperspectral images into their constituent material signatures, or endmembers, and their fractional abundances. Conventional modular approaches estimate the scene composition through successive model-order estimation, endmember extraction, and abundance estimation stages, whose errors can lead to redundant or ambiguous candidate components and ultimately affect the recovered decomposition. We introduce an algorithm-agnostic, large vision-language model (LVLM)-driven agentic framework that refines the outputs of such pipelines rather than replacing their underlying numerical algorithms. Starting from an initial decomposition, the agent iteratively gathers complementary spectral and spatial evidence through dedicated tools, including spectral-library retrieval and abundance-map visualization, and modifies the active endmember set through merge and discard operations followed by abundance re-estimation. We apply the same refinement procedure to several modular pipelines combining different model-order, extraction, and abundance-estimation methods, and evaluate it on HYDICE Urban, Jasper Ridge, and Stonewall Playa. Experiments show that the proposed agent consistently improves endmember cardinality and generally improves the recovered spectral signatures and abundance maps across heterogeneous modular pipelines, while remaining competitive with integrated end-to-end unmixing methods, including CNN-AE, uDAS, and R-CoNMF. These results highlight the potential of tool-using LVLM agents to combine spectral and spatial evidence for algorithm-agnostic refinement of physically grounded hyperspectral unmixing decompositions. Code is publicly available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Uses a large vision-language model as an agent to refine hyperspectral unmixing, which is analogous to astronomical source decomposition and could transfer to JWST spectral analysis.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of hyperspectral unmixing in remote sensing, where mixed pixels are decomposed into material signatures and abundances. The main idea is to use a large vision-language model (LVLM) as an agent that iteratively refines outputs from traditional unmixing pipelines by merging or discarding endmembers based on spectral and spatial evidence. For astronomy, this is relevant because hyperspectral unmixing is similar to decomposing spectra of galaxies or AGN into components, and the agentic approach could be adapted to refine SED fitting or spectral decomposition. A concrete workflow could be using such an agent to refine photometric or spectral decompositions of high-redshift galaxies from JWST data. The caveat is that the paper is tested on remote sensing datasets, not astronomical ones, so transferability needs validation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for details on how the LVLM agent gathers evidence and makes merge/discard decisions
Check if the framework is algorithm-agnostic and could be applied to astronomical spectral fitting tools
See if the tool-use patterns (e.g., spectral library retrieval) have analogs in astronomy
